newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Hutu exodus offers hope but U.N. still sends force.
newsitem.headline: Hutu exodus offers hope but U.N. still sends force.

text.p: The return of thousands of Hutu refugees to Rwanda has given the world its first glimmer of hope in the Zairean crisis but the United Nations still voted to dispatch a multinational humanitarian force.

The crisis, brought to a head by last month's revolt by Tutsi and other Zairean rebels, looked far from solved on Saturday as many more refugees were scattered across eastern Zaire and the region remained a potential war zone.
The 15-member U.N. Security Council on Friday unanimously approved the deployment of the Canadian-led multinational force until March 31 to ensure food and medicine reached refugees.
Canadian ambassador Richard Fowler said the refugee exodus did not exclude the need for a large number of troops.

"Despite the heartening news that up to a third of the Rwandese refugees in Zaire may finally be going home, people will continue to die in eastern Zaire in appalling numbers and their presence there will continue to destablise the region," Fowler told reporters.
"Close to a million refugees will remain at risk, even if the reports of current refugee flows into Gisenyi (Rwanda) are fully accurate," he added.
Fowler said more than 20 countries had offered over 10,000 soldiers.
Rwanda's U.N. ambassador Gideon Kayinamura said the refugee exodus meant the force was no longer relevant and the world should send aid to his country instead.
But U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said the refugees still needed aid and troops were necessary to handle the logistics.
About 700,000 refugees remained "in desperate need of help", she said.
Refugees in the Goma area of eastern Zaire began trekking home on Friday after the departure from amongst their midst of militiamen who had previously prevented them from going home.
The refugees had been held virtual hostage in the huge Mugunga camp, intimidated into staying in exile, until Zairean rebels bombarded it on Thursday.
The Hutu militiamen, blamed for the 1994 genocide of some 800,000 mostly Tutsi people in Rwanda, were reported to have fled into the bush.
As many as 700,000 Hutus, previously crowded into the world's largest refugee camp, joined the march home to Rwanda.
The unexpected exodus came ahead of the U.N. Security Council decision to give legitimacy to a multinational force to aid the estimated 1.2 million Hutu refugees and many displaced Zaireans.
"The impasse has been broken," said Ray Wilkinson of the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR. "This is amazing and unstoppable."
The refugees abandoned the debris of two years of exile and the freshly mutilated bodies of several dozen men, women and children -- deaths some blamed on rebels.
Further west and deeper in Zaire, witnesses reported fighting between Zairean rebels and fleeing Hutu hardliners.

Over a million Hutus fled Rwanda fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide and a civil war in which an army dominated by returning Tutsi exiles took power. Hundreds of thousands of Hutus fled from an equally bitter civil war in Burundi.
The revolt in eastern Zaire, which groups ethnic Tutsis and other opponents of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, has also put hundreds of thousands of Zaireans to flight.
Heavy rain halted Friday's exodus after nightfall. Hoards of refugees huddled at the roadside under plastic sheeting.
With the armed Hutu hardliners moving west, a regrouping of Hutu refugees further inside Zaire remained likely. The whereabouts of many who fled deeper into Zaire earlier was still unclear.
The World Health Organisation confirmed an outbreak of cholera among Zaireans in Sake. Earlier, doctors spoke of cholera among 250,000 refugees near Mwenga in the east.
The logistical problems of dealing with the Hutu influx into Rwanda are huge.

Rwanda's Hutu President Pasteur Bizimungu was at the border to welcome returnees. "We have come here to welcome the people to show them the whole population was waiting for them to reassure them there won't be any harassment," he said.
Zaire says it wants a say on the composition of the force and opposes creation of new refugee camps on its territory. It wants corridors to facilitate the return home of refugees.
"There is no place for any Rwandan refugee in Zaire whoever it is," said Information Minister Boguo Makeli.
The crisis has bred new and deep-seated bitterness.

Zairean Deputy Foreign Minister Lokondo Yoka, speaking in Brussels, accused the Tutsi-dominated armies of Rwanda and Burundi of occupying the eastern towns of Uvira, Bukavu and Goma. "We are determined to wage a total war... We have the means," he said.
